title: Lamentations
subtitle: Eikhah, “How!”
description: Five poems of grief written in the ruins of Jerusalem after the Babylonians burned the city and its temple in 587 or 586 BC, named in Hebrew after their opening cry, “How!” Four of them are acrostics, running through the Hebrew alphabet as if to say this is suffering from first letter to last. The city weeps like a widow with no one to comfort her; the Lord has become like an enemy; children faint in the streets. And at the centre, a man who has seen affliction sits in the ashes and calls to mind that the LORD’s mercies have not failed: “They are new each morning; how great is your faithfulness!” Set out line by line as the poetry it is, in the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Hebrew given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the book’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is the book of Lamentations?
qa.answer: A short Old Testament book of five poems mourning the destruction of Jerusalem and its temple by the Babylonians in 587 or 586 BC. Its Hebrew name, Eikhah, is its first word, a cry meaning “How!” The poems describe the siege and its aftermath without looking away, confess the people’s sin, complain to God and plead with him to look and remember. At the centre stands one of the Bible’s best-loved confessions of hope: “It is by the LORD’s loyal love that we have not been wiped out, for his mercies have not failed. They are new each morning; how great is your faithfulness!” (3:22–23).

qa.question: Who wrote Lamentations, and when?
qa.answer: The book does not name its author. The ancient Greek translation introduces it as a lament of Jeremiah over Jerusalem, and Jewish and Christian tradition long followed this; English Bibles place it after the book of Jeremiah. Jeremiah lived through the fall of the city and is known to have composed laments (2 Chronicles 35:25). Many modern scholars think the poems come from one or more unnamed poets who witnessed the same events. All agree the poems were written soon after the fall of Jerusalem, by people who had seen it.

qa.question: Why is Lamentations written as an acrostic?
qa.answer: The first four poems are alphabetic acrostics: each verse, or in chapter 3 each group of three verses, begins with the next letter of the twenty-two letter Hebrew alphabet. The pattern made the poems easier to learn and to sing, and many readers think it also expresses completeness, grief told from A to Z, and gives order to an experience of chaos. The fifth poem keeps the twenty-two verses but drops the alphabet, as if the pattern itself has broken down while the prayer goes on.

qa.question: Where does the hymn “Great Is Thy Faithfulness” come from?
qa.answer: From Lamentations 3:22–23, translated here “They are new each morning; how great is your faithfulness!” The words are spoken by a man who has just described God’s hand against him in the bleakest terms, and who turns, with nothing in his circumstances changed, by calling to mind God’s loyal love and mercy. The hymn “Great Is Thy Faithfulness”, written by Thomas Chisholm in 1923, took its refrain from this passage.

qa.question: How is Lamentations used in worship?
qa.answer: Jewish communities read Lamentations each year on the fast of the Ninth of Av, which mourns the destruction of the first and second temples, and repeat its next-to-last verse at the end so as not to close on its final words. Christians have long read it during Holy Week, hearing in “Does it mean nothing to you, all you who travel this road?” (1:12) the voice of Christ in his sufferings. Its honest laments have also given many believers words to pray in times of grief.

qa.question: Which translation of the Bible is this?
qa.answer: The Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Hebrew and dedicated to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. Lamentations is poetry throughout, and each line is set on its own; “LORD” in capitals stands for God’s personal name. The reasoning behind each of its sentences, with the Hebrew beside it, is published at openwordbible.org. The introduction and conclusion were written for this edition.
